components.text: Consciousness is the privileged simple category from which reality should be reduced.
Beginning from the pre-theoretical datum yields a preferable explanatory account of nature.
Consciousness is treated as the sole pre-theoretical datum.
Beginning from consciousness is claimed to yield the preferable reductive ontology.
Idealism must preserve a world whose existence and behavior do not depend on individual wishes.
Idealism must explain how an external structured world differs from private experience.
The hard problem motivates rejection of physical-to-mental emergence and dualism.
The unknown monistic basis need not be identified specifically as mental.
Idealism must explain differentiation between individual and external states.
Idealism must explain the world's stable physical structure and behavior.
External mental states exist independently and are inaccessible except through perceptual representation.
Labeling those represented states mental avoids adding a separate ontological category.
The account must explain the origin and construction of structured representations.
The external world is independent of individual observers and their private contents.
Perception is an internal representation of an inaccessible external substrate.
The represented external substrate is specifically mental rather than ontologically neutral.
Calling the external substrate mental must add explanatory value rather than merely rename it.
The account must explain how external states affect and generate internal representations.
Calling the external substrate mental appears to add no explanatory value.
The source and machinery of perceptual representations remain unexplained.
Individual mental states are separated from the external world's mental states.
The separation permits external states to affect internal states through perception.
Removing a nonmental category is claimed to dissolve the hard problem.
Dissociated internal states receive information through a boundary from external states.
The account must identify what constitutes the internal-external boundary.
The boundary must connect intelligibly with bodies and their observable properties.
Idealism must explain why differentiated subjects or regions arise.
Idealism must account for stable physical structure and repeatable behavior.
A sharp division between internal and external mental states is presupposed.
The source and bodily manifestation of that boundary require explanation.
A monist ontology can preserve causal and physical regularity without nonmental substance.
External mentality has intrinsic dispositions that explain predictable physical behavior.
Only removal of a nonmental category is claimed to avoid the hard problem.
Mental-to-mental causation is offered as the machinery of representation.
There is something it is like to be a representation or model rather than a persisting physical self.
The representational reframe avoids the hard problem without committing to idealism.
The neutral-monist version need not claim that only neuroactivity exists.
Neutral monism is distinguished from materialist or dualist emergence theories.
Experience is located in a subject's representational model rather than a separately assumed physical subject.
The representational move is claimed to avoid the hard problem.
The persisting personal self is a delusive conscious model rather than a stable agent.
The experienced existence of models supports the conclusion that consciousness is ontologically fundamental.
Materialist model accounts face a regress because each explanatory model would itself be neuroactivity.
Experienced representational models still instantiate mentality.
The apparently persisting personal self can be a constructed model or delusion.
Materialist illusionism fails because modeling only postpones the experiential problem.
